partners.mechanism_chain: SERPING1 (HGNC:10536) —DISRUPTS→ Complement system activation (GO:0006955); SERPING1 (HGNC:10536) —DISRUPTS→ Kinin-Kallikrein System (REACT:R-HSA-5689439); KNG1 (HGNC:6345) —DISRUPTS→ Kinin-Kallikrein System (REACT:R-HSA-5689439); Kinin-Kallikrein System (REACT:R-HSA-5689439) —INCREASES→ Bradykinin (CHEBI:16817); Bradykinin (CHEBI:16817) —LEADS_TO→ Angioedema (HP:0002787); Bradykinin (CHEBI:16817) —LEADS_TO→ Edema (HP:0002088). Loss-of-function mutations in SERPING1 (C1 inhibitor deficiency) and KNG1 (hereditary angioedema 6) both lead to dysregulation of the kallikrein-kinin system. SERPING1 normally inhibits C1 esterase, a component of the complement system that also activates Factor XII, which in turn activates prekallikrein to kallikrein. Kallikrein then cleaves high-molecular-weight kininogen to produce bradykinin. KNG1 encodes high-molecular-weight kininogen, the precursor to bradykinin. Deficiencies in C1 inhibitor (SERPING1) lead to uncontrolled activation of both the complement and kallikrein systems, resulting in elevated bradykinin. Similarly, defects in KNG1 directly impair bradykinin production, but its absence or altered function in some contexts can lead to increased bradykinin availability or reduced degradation. The resulting excess of bradykinin increases vascular permeability, leading to angioedema and edema.

Gain-of-function mutations in APP lead to increased production of amyloid-beta peptides, which in turn activate the complement system, contributing to Alzheimer disease pathology.

**How to falsify it:** If genetic studies show that mutations in SERPING1 do not lead to decreased C1 inhibitor function or that APP mutations do not lead to increased amyloid-beta production or complement activation, this hypothesis would be falsified. Additionally, if common variants in SERPING1 or APP are found at a high frequency (>1%) in gnomAD and are associated with either disease, it would weaken the causal link. _(variant: rs1049296)_

**Why it matters:** Understanding the shared role of complement dysregulation could lead to novel therapeutic strategies targeting the complement cascade for both hereditary angioedema and Alzheimer disease. For instance, inhibitors of complement component C5, which are already used for HAE, might have potential benefits in AD.
